sections.h2: La Paz County at a glance
sections.html:
Out on Arizona's western edge, La Paz County has a small tax base and a lot of open space: 4,514 square miles and 16,557 residents at the 2020 count. Parker is the seat and biggest town, with Quartzsite the only other incorporated town, and the Colorado River Indian Reservation takes up the western side.

The census found 13,457 housing units in 2020. Of those, 45.2% stood vacant, and 71.8% of occupied homes were occupied by their owners. Mobile homes are common, and the Assessor's office keeps the records for them. Ownership is updated from Motor Vehicle Division title records, and the roll cannot change until a new title is issued. Until then, the previous owner keeps receiving the notice of value and the tax bill. If you are selling a mobile home, check that the title has actually been transferred.

Property tax here is a two-office job. The La Paz County Assessor handles value, ownership, parcel maps, exemptions, mobile homes and business personal property. The La Paz County Treasurer sends the bills and takes the payments. Because the Assessor sets no rates, mails no bills and neither collects nor refunds money, you call the Treasurer about an amount due and the Assessor about a value.

  • Treasurer: 1112 Joshua Avenue, Suite 203, Parker, AZ 85344. Hours are Monday through Thursday, 7:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., with Fridays closed.
  • Assessor: 1112 Joshua Avenue, Suite 204, Parker, AZ 85344, phone 928-669-6165.
  • Recorder: 928-669-6136, for deeds and recording fee questions.

Deed details come to the Assessor from the Recorder, and permit details come from La Paz County Community Development, the Town of Parker and the Town of Quartzsite. A room added or a roof lost without a permit can still surface on the roll later, so put your permit paperwork in the sale file.

The year's tax is paid in halves, one due October 1 and one March 1 (A.R.S. 42-18052). The Treasurer counts a payment late after 6:00 p.m. on the delinquency date, and postmarked payments are accepted. Expect a minimum payment of $10 or 10% of the tax due, whichever is greater.

DateWhat happens
October 1First half due. Bills go out by mail in September.
Early November, 6:00 p.m.First half delinquent
December 31, 2026Last day to pay the full year and avoid interest
March 1, 2027Second half due
May 4, 2027, 6:00 p.m.Second half delinquent

If the first half is still unpaid, interest is already running. Paying the whole year by December 31 stops further interest under A.R.S. 42-18053, so a seller who closes in December can clear it at the table.

Late tax grows at 16% per year, simple, beginning on the delinquency date, and any part of a month is billed as a full month (A.R.S. 42-18053). The Treasurer applies that 16% in monthly steps from the first of the month until payment.

Three cases carry no interest:

  • The assessor or treasurer made the error that caused the delinquency.
  • You pay the whole year's tax by December 31 of the tax year.
  • The year after a mortgage or deed of trust was released, the treasurer can waive interest and penalties once per property, with board of supervisors approval.

For a sale, ask the Treasurer for a payoff that holds through your closing date. Parcel search and card payments are on the Treasurer's website. Paying by Visa debit adds $4.00, a credit card adds 2.55%, and the jurisdiction code you give over the phone is 1312.

Disagree with the notice? Petition the County Assessor within 60 days of the day it was mailed. A.R.S. 42-16051 sets that limit and treats the postmark as your filing date. Owners of record get a notice each year, and only the full cash value or the property class may be challenged.

In the petition, give your opinion of full cash value with substantial supporting information. Arizona recognizes three methods: income, market and cost. The market method calls for at least one comparable property or the sale of your own property. If you bought or sold recently at arm's length, that sale is your strongest evidence.

Note that limited property value is a different figure. Proposition 117 holds its growth to 5% a year, with exceptions found in A.R.S. Title 42, Chapter 13, Article 7. Bills run on limited value, so a rise in full cash value does not always lift your tax by the same amount.

Two programs are run through the Assessor, and the office can give you the current income and value limits. Call 928-669-6165 before you list.

  • Exemption for widows, widowers and totally disabled persons age 17 or over. You must live in Arizona, meet income requirements, and stay under an indexed assessed-value limit. A disability claim needs a physician's certification that the disability is total and permanent.
  • Senior Property Valuation Protection, often called the senior freeze. It freezes limited property value for three years. You must be 65 at the time of application, use the home as your primary Arizona residence, and meet income rules.

A value can jump when a buyer takes over a home whose prior owner held a senior freeze, so a buyer should expect a first notice of value that looks higher than the seller's. Owners of short-term rentals should also look at the rental registration form on the Assessor's page and the state's online lodging marketplace registration.

The tax lien attaches on January 1 of the tax year (A.R.S. 42-17153). Only state liens and tax liens from other years outrank it. It lasts until taxes, penalties, charges and interest are paid, a buyer takes title at a tax sale, or a certificate of removal and abatement is issued. Expect the buyer's title company to want the current year and any earlier years cleared out of your proceeds.

Owing tax is routine at a sale as long as the numbers are clear. Follow this order:

  1. Request a payoff from the Treasurer dated for your closing.
  2. Check the owner of record with the Assessor.
  3. Hand both figures to the title company.
  4. Sign the deed with its sworn affidavit of property value under A.R.S. 11-1133. The recorder must refuse the deed without it unless an exemption is noted.

The Recorder posts its document rules online: paper 8 1/2 inches wide and 11 to 14 inches long, a two-inch top margin on page one, ink signatures in the original, and the correct fee. Call 928-669-6136 for the fee schedule. With a cash buyer, there is no lender timeline, so the county payoff is often the one open item left.

faqs.q: What happens if I do not pay the first half of my La Paz County tax?
faqs.a: It goes delinquent and 16% annual interest starts building. Settling the whole year by December 31, 2026 stops more interest, under A.R.S. 42-18053.

faqs.q: Where do I pay La Paz County property tax?
faqs.a: Pay the County Treasurer at 1112 Joshua Avenue, Suite 203, Parker, Arizona 85344, by mail or in person, or pay online or by phone. The office is open Monday through Thursday, 7:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., and closed Fridays. Card payments add a $4.00 fee on Visa debit or 2.55% on credit cards.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my La Paz County notice of value?
faqs.a: You get sixty days, counted from the day the Assessor mailed it. The petition goes to the County Assessor, and under A.R.S. 42-16051 your postmark is the filing date.

faqs.q: Does La Paz County have a senior property tax freeze?
faqs.a: Yes. Senior Property Valuation Protection freezes limited property value for three years. The owner must be 65 at application, use the home as a primary Arizona residence, and meet income limits. Call the Assessor at 928-669-6165 for the form and current limits.

faqs.q: Can I sell a La Paz County house that still has tax due?
faqs.a: Yes, and it happens often. Closing pays the lien from your proceeds. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff for your closing date, because interest runs monthly on delinquent amounts, and pass it to the title company.
